Read The Body
ECG, EMG, EEG, and optical pulse — six builds that pull a living signal out of
a room full of noise. From a $15 sensor that finds your heartbeat in a beam of
light to a robotic hand that closes when you flex, to catching an 8 Hz rhythm
from your own visual cortex. Cheap parts; real precision analog.

❯ project 01
Optical Pulse Sensor (PPG)
Shine light through your finger and watch your heartbeat appear

$15
beginner
1 weekend
## why this matters

The gentlest way into biosignals uses no electrodes at all. Shine light into tissue and a
photodiode sees it dim slightly with every heartbeat, because each pulse of blood absorbs a
little more. That is photoplethysmography (PPG) — the exact sensor on the back of every
smartwatch and fitness ring. A $5 module gives you a raw optical waveform; your job is to
pull the tiny pulsatile component out of a big steady one, filter it, and count peaks into a
heart rate. It teaches the AC-on-DC structure that runs through every biosignal in this
guide, without ever touching a skin electrode.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand photoplethysmography, separating a small AC signal riding on a large DC
baseline, band-pass filtering, peak detection, and why motion artifacts dominate
wearable sensing — the core of consumer health-device engineering.

→ the job this maps to: wearables and consumer health-device engineering — smartwatch,
fitness-tracker, and ring companies.

! NOT A PULSE OXIMETER
This shows a pulse waveform and a heart rate. It is not a medical instrument. Real SpO₂
readings require empirical calibration against a clinical reference on actual subjects —
a number your build cannot produce trustworthily. Never make a health decision from it,
and if you are worried about your heart or breathing, see a doctor, not a breadboard.

Light in, blood out: An LED sends light into the tissue and a photodiode measures how much
comes back. Blood volume rises with each heartbeat and absorbs more light, so the detected
signal dips in time with your pulse.

AC riding on DC: Most of what the photodiode sees is constant — skin, bone, static blood.
The heartbeat is a tiny fluctuation (the AC part) on top of that big DC level. Extracting a
clean AC from a dominant DC is the whole game.

Why green for heart rate: Green light is strongly absorbed by haemoglobin and penetrates
shallowly, giving a strong pulse signal with less motion sensitivity. That is why fitness
wearables glow green on your wrist.

Red and infrared for oxygenation: Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin absorb red
(~660 nm) and infrared (~940 nm) light differently. Comparing the pulsatile signal at both
wavelengths is how commercial pulse oximeters estimate SpO₂ — but only after calibration
against a clinical reference.

Band-pass and peak detect: A heart rate lives around 0.7–3 Hz (40–180 bpm). Band-pass the
signal into that window to kill DC drift and high-frequency noise, then detect peaks and
time the intervals to get beats per minute.

## build steps
## interview questions
Read the raw sensor

Wire the MAX30102 over I2C, load the library, and stream the raw red and IR counts. Rest
a fingertip on it and confirm the numbers wobble slightly with each heartbeat.
Plot the waveform

Stream the raw values to a plot. You should see a large baseline with a small ripple —
that ripple is your pulse. Note how much bigger the DC part is than the AC part.
Filter to the pulse band

Band-pass roughly 0.7–3 Hz to remove the DC baseline and high-frequency noise. The
waveform should now show clean, repeating pulse peaks.
Count the beats

Detect peaks, measure the interval between them, and convert to beats per minute.
Compare to your pulse counted by hand at the wrist to sanity-check the number.
Break it on purpose

Move your finger, press harder, press lighter, and watch the signal collapse into motion
artifact. Understanding why wearables struggle during exercise is the real lesson here.

❯ project 02
Biopotential Front End
The instrumentation amplifier that pulls a 1 mV signal out of a room full of mains hum

$20
intermediate
1 weekend
## why this matters

Your body produces electrical signals measured in millivolts — and it also acts as an antenna
that picks up the mains hum flooding every room, often a thousand times larger than the
signal you want. The instrumentation amplifier is the circuit that solves this: it amplifies
only the difference between two electrodes while rejecting everything they see in common. Add
a driven-reference electrode and careful filtering and suddenly a heartbeat or a muscle
twitch emerges from the noise. This is the single circuit that makes ECG, EMG, and EEG
possible, and building it yourself — rather than buying a module — is what separates people
who understand biosignals from people who plug in a breakout board.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand instrumentation-amplifier topology, common-mode rejection (CMRR), driven-
reference (right-leg drive) circuits, electrode half-cell offsets and why you must AC-
couple, gain staging, and mains-hum rejection — the foundation of all precision
biomedical analog design.

→ the job this maps to: medical-device and precision-analog engineering — patient-monitoring,
diagnostics, and analog front-end teams.

! BATTERY POWER, ALWAYS — AND NEVER INJECT CURRENT
Anything wired to your skin must run on batteries and must never be connected to mains-
powered gear (a plugged-in laptop, a bench scope, a wall adapter) while electrodes are
on a body. Use series resistors in every electrode lead, and isolate (Bluetooth, or an
unplugged battery laptop) if you need to see the data on a computer. Everything in this
guide only measures — never build anything that pushes current into a person, and do not
attach electrodes to anyone with a pacemaker or implanted device.

The signal is tiny, the noise is huge: An ECG is about 1 mV, an EMG a few mV, an EEG only
tens of microvolts. Meanwhile your body couples capacitively to mains wiring and carries
volts of 50 / 60 Hz interference. The signal is buried a thousandfold.

Differential rescue: That interference appears almost identically on both measuring
electrodes (it is common-mode), while the biosignal appears as a difference between them.
An instrumentation amplifier amplifies the difference and rejects the common part — its
ability to do so is its CMRR.

Driven reference (right-leg drive): Better still, sense the common-mode voltage on the
body, invert it, and feed it back through a third electrode. This actively cancels the
interference at the source and buys you far more rejection than the amplifier alone —
without ever tying the body to ground.

Electrode offsets force AC coupling: Two Ag/AgCl electrodes on skin produce a DC half-cell
voltage of up to a few hundred millivolts — hundreds of times bigger than the signal. If
you applied full gain to that, the amplifier would slam into its rail. So you take modest
gain first, high-pass to strip the DC, then apply the rest of the gain.

Filtering to the band you want: Each biosignal has a band: ECG roughly 0.5–40 Hz, EMG
roughly 20–450 Hz, EEG roughly 1–30 Hz. Band-pass to that window (plus an optional 50 /
60 Hz notch) and you throw away most of the remaining noise.

## build steps
## interview questions
Build the amplifier core

Wire the instrumentation amp with a modest first-stage gain (about 10). Power it from
batteries only. Test it with a signal generator or a divider before it ever touches
skin.
Add series lead resistors

Put a current-limiting resistor (tens of kΩ) in each electrode lead. This is a safety
measure, not an optional extra, and it costs you nothing in signal quality.
AC-couple and add gain

High-pass at roughly 0.5 Hz to strip the electrode DC offset, then add a second gain
stage (100 or more) plus a low-pass for your band. Confirm the output no longer
saturates.
Add the driven reference

Buffer and invert the common-mode voltage and drive it back into a third electrode on a
bony spot (hip or elbow). Watch the mains hum on your output collapse — this is the most
satisfying moment in the build.
Prove it on a real signal

Put two electrodes across your forearm, clench your fist, and watch the burst of muscle
activity. You now have the front end that every remaining project in this guide depends
on.

❯ project 03
ECG Heart Monitor
Watch your own heartbeat draw itself on screen, wave by wave

$25
intermediate
1 weekend
## why this matters

Every beat of your heart is a coordinated electrical wave, and it is large enough to read
from your skin. Put two electrodes across your chest or arms, run them into a biopotential
front end, and the classic PQRST complex appears on screen: the small P wave as the atria
fire, the sharp QRS spike as the ventricles contract, the broad T wave as they reset. Then
detect those R peaks and you have a live heart rate and beat-to-beat variability. It is the
most iconic biosignal there is, the payoff is unmistakable, and it is the project that proves
you can build precision analog that works on a living system.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand cardiac electrophysiology at the signal level, lead configurations, the
ECG bandwidth, R-peak detection algorithms, heart-rate and HRV extraction, and safe
patient-connected design — the exact skill set of medical-device and patient-monitoring
engineering.

→ the job this maps to: medical-device engineering — patient monitoring, cardiac diagnostics,
and clinical-instrumentation teams.

! NOT A MEDICAL DEVICE
This is an engineering demonstration, not a diagnostic tool. It is not calibrated, not
validated, and not certified. It can show you a waveform and a heart rate; it cannot
tell you whether your heart is healthy, and a normal-looking trace means nothing
clinically. Never make a health decision from it. If you have any cardiac concern, see a
doctor.

## how it works

BUILD NOTE
The AD8232 packages the whole front end — instrumentation amp, right-leg drive, and
filters — into one $10 chip. Start there to get a waveform fast, then rebuild it with
your project-2 front end to prove you understand what the chip is doing.
## key design decisions

The heart as a moving dipole: As the cardiac muscle depolarises, it creates an electrical
wavefront that behaves like a rotating dipole in your torso. Electrodes on the skin see the
projection of that dipole — which is why where you place them changes what you see.

Reading the PQRST: The P wave is atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex is the much larger
ventricular depolarisation, and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. Their shapes and
timings are what clinicians read; for you, the tall R peak is the easiest landmark.

Leads and placement: Einthoven’s triangle defines the classic limb leads. Lead I runs right
arm to left arm; Lead II (right arm to left leg) usually gives the biggest, cleanest R peak
— a good first target. A third electrode carries the driven reference.

The right bandwidth: Monitoring-grade ECG lives roughly between 0.5 and 40 Hz. Band-pass
there and you remove electrode drift below and muscle noise above, without mangling the QRS
shape.

Finding the beats: The classic R-peak detector (Pan-Tompkins) band-passes the signal,
differentiates it, squares it, integrates over a moving window, and thresholds the result.
Time the intervals between R peaks and you have heart rate and beat-to-beat variability.

Why not just notch out the mains hum and skip the fancy front end? A notch filter removes
interference after the amplifier — but if the hum is a thousand times larger than the
signal, it has already saturated your gain stages and the ECG is unrecoverable. And a notch
near the QRS band distorts the waveform. The real fix is rejecting the interference at the
input, with CMRR and a driven reference, so it never gets amplified in the first place.

Why drive a reference electrode instead of just grounding the body? Tying a person to
circuit ground creates a low-impedance path for fault current — a safety hazard — and it
does not actually cancel the common-mode voltage. A driven-reference electrode feeds back
an inverted copy of the common-mode signal through a high-value resistor, actively
cancelling the hum while keeping the connection current-limited and safe.

Why AC-couple when the ECG has low-frequency content? Electrode half-cell offsets reach
hundreds of millivolts against a 1 mV signal, so without a high-pass the amplifier rails
and you see nothing at all. The compromise is to set the corner low (about 0.5 Hz) — enough
to strip electrode drift while preserving the ECG’s slow features like the T wave.

it. Compare to your pulse counted by hand, then watch the rate rise after a set of push-

❯ project 04
EMG Muscle Sensor
Clench your fist and watch the electrical storm in your forearm

$25
intermediate
1 weekend
## why this matters

When you contract a muscle, hundreds of motor units fire and their summed action potentials
reach the skin as surface EMG — a burst of noisy, high-frequency activity whose amplitude
tracks how hard you are pushing. Reuse your biopotential front end, shift the filter band
upward, rectify and smooth the result, and you get a clean “muscle effort” signal you can
plot, threshold, or use as a control input. It is the biosignal most useful as an interface,
and it is the direct prerequisite for the myoelectric hand in project 5.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand surface EMG generation, why its band differs from ECG, envelope detection
(rectify plus low-pass), electrode placement along muscle fibres, crosstalk between
adjacent muscles, and turning a biosignal into a usable control value — the basis of
human-machine interface work.

→ the job this maps to: biomedical sensing and human-machine interface engineering — neural-
wearable, rehab-tech, and gesture-input teams.
## how it works

Where the signal comes from: A motor neuron fires and the muscle fibres it controls
depolarise. Thousands of these overlapping action potentials sum into a noisy, spiky
voltage at the skin — a few hundred microvolts to a few millivolts, much rougher-looking
than an ECG.

A different band: Most EMG energy sits between about 20 and 450 Hz. High-passing at ~20 Hz
is essential: it rejects motion artifact and the ECG contamination that would otherwise
pollute a recording taken anywhere near the torso.

The envelope is the useful part: Raw EMG looks like noise, and its instantaneous value is
meaningless for control. Rectify it (take the absolute value) and low-pass it, and you get
a smooth envelope whose height tracks contraction strength — that is the signal you
actually use.

Placement and crosstalk: Put two electrodes on the belly of the target muscle, aligned with
the fibre direction, with a reference on a bony landmark. Place them poorly and you will
pick up neighbouring muscles — crosstalk, the main reason multi-gesture control is hard.

Fatigue and drift: As a muscle tires, the EMG amplitude and frequency content shift, so a
fixed threshold that worked ten minutes ago may not work now. Real systems recalibrate or
normalise — a lesson that matters immediately in project 5.

Retune the front end

Take your project-2 amplifier and move the band to roughly 20–450 Hz. Everything else —

Place the electrodes

Plot the raw signal. Relaxed, it should be near-silent; contracting, it should explode

Build the envelope

Rectify the signal and low-pass it (a few Hz) to produce a smooth envelope. Squeeze
gently, then hard, and confirm the envelope height tracks your effort.
Turn it into a control

Map the envelope to something visible — an LED’s brightness, a bar graph, a servo angle.
Set a threshold for “muscle on,” then check how well it holds up as your arm tires.

❯ project 05
EMG-Controlled Robotic Hand
Flex your forearm and a robotic hand closes — myoelectric control, built on your bench

$70
advanced
2 weekends
## why this matters

This is the build that makes people stop scrolling. Take the EMG envelope from project 4, map
it to servo positions, and a tendon-driven robotic hand opens and closes in time with your
own muscle — the same myoelectric principle behind real prosthetic limbs. Add a second EMG
channel (flexor and extensor) and you can command open and close independently; map the
envelope proportionally and the grip strength follows your effort. It ties every skill in
this guide together into a single, visceral demo: biology in, mechanics out.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You can take a noisy biological signal all the way through a real system —
amplification, filtering, envelope extraction, calibration, thresholding, and actuator
control — and make it work in real time on a living body. That end-to-end biosignal-to-
actuator pipeline is exactly what prosthetics and neural-interface teams build.

→ the job this maps to: prosthetics, neural interfaces, and robotics — prosthetic-limb
makers, neural-wearable companies, and rehab-robotics teams.

## how it works

BUILD NOTE
Don’t design a hand from scratch. Print an open-source tendon-driven hand (InMoov and
similar) or buy a servo hand kit, drive the fingers with fishing line, and power the
servos from their own supply — not from the microcontroller’s rail, which will brown out
the moment five servos move at once.

Envelope to angle: The EMG envelope is a single number tracking contraction strength. Map
it to a servo position and the finger closes as you squeeze harder — proportional
myoelectric control, in one line of arithmetic.

Two channels, two commands: One electrode pair on your flexor (closing) and another on your
extensor (opening) gives you two independent inputs, so you can command open and close
deliberately rather than relying on one muscle relaxing.

Calibration is mandatory: Everyone’s EMG amplitude differs, and it drifts with sweat,
electrode position, and fatigue. Every session starts with a calibration: record a relaxed
baseline and a maximum contraction, then normalise everything in between.

Tendon-driven mechanics: Five servos pull fishing-line tendons through the fingers, with
elastic returning them. The mechanics are simple and the compliance is forgiving — which is
exactly why this architecture is so common in hobby and research hands alike.

What real prosthetics add: Clinical myoelectric limbs use multi-channel EMG plus pattern-
recognition machine learning to classify many grips, with socket fitting, robustness, and
regulatory validation on top. Your build is the honest core of that idea, and the rest is
engineering rigour.

## build steps
## interview questions
Build the hand

Print or assemble the tendon-driven hand, route fishing line through each finger to a
servo horn, and add elastic returns. Test each finger by driving its servo directly —
mechanics first, biology second.
Separate your power

Run the servos from their own 5 V supply with a common ground to the logic, and keep the
EMG front end on its own isolated battery. Servo current spikes will wreck a shared rail
and inject noise into your biosignal.
Feed in one EMG channel

Take the envelope from project 4 and map it to grip position. Clench and watch the hand
close. Expect it to be jittery — that is the raw truth of biosignals.
Calibrate and smooth

Record your relaxed baseline and maximum contraction, normalise the envelope between
them, add hysteresis so it does not chatter at the threshold, and smooth the servo
motion. It should now feel deliberate.
Add the second channel

Add an extensor channel so one muscle closes and the other opens. Tune both, then film
it — a hand that mirrors your own muscle in real time is the single best portfolio clip
in this guide.

❯ project 06
EEG Alpha-Wave Detector
Close your eyes and watch an 8 to 12 Hz rhythm rise out of the noise

$60
advanced
2 weekends
## why this matters

EEG is the hardest biosignal there is: tens of microvolts, a hundred times smaller than an
ECG, buried under mains hum, muscle tension, and eye movement. But there is one effect a
careful DIY rig can genuinely capture — the alpha rhythm. Relax with your eyes closed and an
8 to 12 Hz oscillation appears over the back of your head; open your eyes and it vanishes
within a second. Watching that band power rise and fall on an FFT, on command, is the most
demanding and most rewarding build in this guide — and it is a real, reproducible
neuroscience result, not a gimmick.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You can design a genuinely low-noise, high-gain analog front end, manage shielding and
grounding at the microvolt level, distinguish real neural signal from muscle and eye
artifact, and validate a result experimentally. Microvolt-level analog design and honest
artifact rejection are precisely what neurotech teams look for.

→ the job this maps to: neurotech and brain-computer interface engineering — BCI startups,
neural-wearable companies, and neuroscience research labs.

! IT WILL NOT READ YOUR MIND
Alpha blocking — a rhythm that appears when your eyes close and disappears when they
open — is the realistic and honest goal. Anything claiming to read thoughts or emotions
from a few electrodes is overselling. Most hobby “brainwave” projects are actually
detecting jaw clenching or eye blinks; the eyes-closed alpha test is how you prove yours
is real. This is also not a diagnostic device, and it cannot tell you anything about
your neurological health.

## how it works

BUILD NOTE
This is the one build where sloppiness guarantees failure. Battery power, shielded
leads, short wires, a driven reference, and real electrode contact (gold cup electrodes
with conductive paste, parted through the hair) are not optional extras — they are the
difference between alpha waves and a screen full of mains hum.

Microvolts, not millivolts: Scalp EEG is roughly 10–100 µV — ten to a hundred times smaller
than an ECG. That means much higher gain (often 10,000× or more), far lower noise, and no
tolerance for the sloppy wiring you got away with earlier.

The alpha rhythm: When a relaxed person closes their eyes, neurons in the visual cortex
synchronise into an 8–12 Hz oscillation that is strongest over the occipital region, at the
back of the head. Opening the eyes suppresses it almost immediately. This alpha blocking is
the classic, reproducible EEG demonstration.

Electrodes and placement: Measure over the occipital area, referenced to an earlobe or
mastoid, with a driven reference electrode. Gold cup electrodes with conductive paste
(parted through the hair) give far better contact than dry electrodes — and contact quality
dominates your result.

Artifacts everywhere: Eye blinks produce huge slow deflections, jaw and neck tension
produce broadband muscle noise, and any cable movement produces artifact. All of these are
bigger than the alpha you are chasing, which is why so many “brainwave” demos are really
artifact detectors.

Proving it with an FFT: Band-pass roughly 1–30 Hz, run an FFT, and watch the power in the
8–12 Hz bin. Eyes closed and relaxed: it rises. Eyes open: it drops. Toggling that on
command, repeatably, is your proof the signal is neural and not noise.

## build steps
## interview questions
Build for noise, not speed

Assemble the front end with very high gain, split across stages, band-passed to about 1–
30 Hz with a mains notch. Keep leads short and shielded and run everything from
batteries in a shielded enclosure.
Prove the rig on ECG first

Before you go near your head, record an ECG with the same rig. If you cannot get a clean
ECG, you will never see EEG — this step will save you a weekend of confusion.
Place occipital electrodes
Sit still, close your eyes

Relax, stay very still, and record with eyes closed for thirty seconds, then eyes open
for thirty seconds. Stillness matters enormously — any jaw tension will swamp the
signal.
Find the alpha in the FFT

Run an FFT and compare the 8–12 Hz band power between the two conditions. A clear rise
with eyes closed, repeatable across trials, is real alpha. Anything that only appears
when you blink or clench is artifact — be honest about which you got.

❯ wrap

Your body is broadcasting —
most engineers just can’t hear it.

A pulse in a beam of light, a heartbeat across your chest, a muscle firing, a rhythm in your
visual cortex — six ways to pull a living signal out of noise a thousand times larger. The
parts are cheap (a $5 optical sensor, a $6 instrumentation amp, a pack of electrodes). The
skill is entirely in the analog: the common-mode rejection, the gain staging, the filtering,
the honest separation of signal from artifact. That is exactly what medical-device,
neurotech, and wearable teams hire for.
// the skill ladder
Build them in order and each one hands you the technique the next one needs:
optical pulse →biopotential front end →ECG →EMG →myoelectric control →EEG

! THE RULES, EVERY SINGLE TIME
Battery power only. Never connect a body-attached circuit to mains-powered equipment —
no plugged-in laptop, no bench scope, no wall adapter. Put current-limiting resistors in
every electrode lead, and isolate (Bluetooth, or a laptop running on battery) if you
need the data on a computer. Everything here only measures; never build anything that
pushes current into a person, and never attach electrodes to anyone with a pacemaker or
implanted device. And none of these are medical devices — they are demonstrations, and
no health decision should ever come from one.

DO THIS
Build even one. Capture the trace — a PQRST complex, an EMG envelope tracking your grip,
a hand closing when you flex, alpha power rising when your eyes close — and put the code
on GitHub with your filter design, your calibration, and an honest note on artifacts and
scope. One biosignal demo and one clean repo prove you can do precision analog on a
living system.

Full build notes, parts links, and the next field guide go out in The Build List. The
people actually shipping these — and trading electrode and shielding tricks — are in
Ohm’s Club.
